tier_rationale: Manufacturer's own product page describes a floor-standing steamer built around a 1300W brass heating element, a 3/4-gallon water tank, and a hose to a steam head — the page explicitly notes there is 'no need for a temperature setting like on an iron,' i.e. the only control is on/off. No WiFi, Bluetooth, app, or connectivity feature is mentioned. No FCC grantee record exists for Jiffy Steamer at all, consistent with a manufacturer whose entire product line (garment steamers essentially unchanged since the 1940s) has never included a radio.
the_unplug_test: Nothing changes. Fill the tank, plug the unit into a wall outlet, and flip it on; steam flows continuously through the hose until you turn it off. There is no temperature dial, no app, and no account anywhere in the design — a Jiffy Steamer from decades ago works the same way as one bought today.

repairability.notes: Steam heads, hoses, and casters are sold as separate configurable options and replacement parts directly by the manufacturer. 3-year limited warranty, UL/cUL/TUV listed.

sources.supports: Manufacturer product page for the J-2000 (item #12315): 1300W solid brass heating element, 3/4-gallon reservoir (~1.5 hours continuous steam), 5.5-foot hose, 360-degree casters, $289.00, 3-year limited warranty, UL/cUL/TUV/GS/CE listed. States the steamer needs 'no temperature setting like on an iron' — i.e. its only control is on/off. No WiFi, app, or connectivity feature mentioned anywhere on the page.

open_questions: Could not locate any FCC grantee record for Jiffy Steamer Co. at all, meaning there is no sibling grant to compare against (unlike the Speed Queen/Bissell/eufy records in this batch) — the absence is consistent with, but not independent confirmation of, no radio ever being present in any Jiffy product.
This record supports one Class A source only; a second independent source (a distributor spec sheet or a service manual) would strengthen it further.
notes: Jiffy Steamer has made continuous-flow garment steamers of essentially this same mechanical design since the 1940s and sells to dry cleaners, tailors, and costume/wardrobe departments as much as to home buyers — a light-commercial product line with no incentive to add connectivity.
